# Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (Snp 2.13 (PTS Snp 63))

**ID:** Snp 2.13 (PTS Snp 63)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Right Way to Wander
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp2.13
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta* is the thirteenth discourse of the *Cūḷavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* (verses 359–375, PTS Snp 63) [Anderson & Smith 1913; Norman 1997-2001]. The commentary *Paramatthajotikā II* notes that the discourse was also known as the *Mahāsamaya Sutta* because it was delivered on the occasion of the "great assembly" (*mahāsamaya*) when a multitude of deities had gathered [Anderson & Smith 1913; Norman 1997-2001; Tournier et al. 2018]. According to this commentary, the discourse is framed as a dialogue between the historical Buddha and a conjured or illusory Buddha (*nimmitabuddha*): the magical Buddha asks the opening question in the first stanza, the Buddha delivers his response across fifteen stanzas, and the interlocutor praises him in the seventeenth and final stanza [Tournier et al. 2018].

The sutta addresses the conduct and spiritual stance of the mendicant who, having left the household life and rejected sense pleasures, wanders through the world [Anderson & Smith 1913; Saddhatissa 2013; Jennings 1948]. Sixteen of the seventeen stanzas close with the characteristic refrain *sammā so loke paribbajeyya* ("he should wander rightly in the world") [Bailey & Mabbett 2003]. The verses emphasize complete detachment, self-reliance, and freedom from factional strife: the mendicant must be independent (*anissito*), not led by others, and refrain from taking sides among factious groups (*vaggagatesu na vaggasārī*, v. 371) [Powers 2016; Bailey & Mabbett 2003]. The ideal wanderer sheds beliefs in portents, dreams, and divination [Jennings 1948], harbors no ill-will even when cursed [Arnold & Bowden 1900], and—as noted in commentary on Āryaśūra's *Jātakamālā*—exemplifies an earnest practitioner who may even be described as a *buddha* or *muni* (v. 370 / v. 12) [Speyer 1895]. In Burma, the text was also incorporated into the expanded *Catubhāṇavāra* (*Paritta*) liturgy [Kalupahana 2001].

Within the Pali tradition, the sutta is referenced in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2, *Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi*) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus records Pali-internal text reuse primarily with the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* (11 matches) and the *Dīghanikāye Mahāvaggaṭīkā* (5 matches) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus identifies 12 matches with the Sanskrit *Patna Dharmapada* (scoring up to 75) and extensive correspondences with the Tibetan translation of the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra* (D0287) [DharmaNexus].
